question_text: A 15-year-old teenager presents for a sports physical. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), and heart rate is 100/min. On cardiac auscultation, an early diastolic heart sound is heard over the cardiac apex while the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position. A transthoracic echocardiogram is performed which shows an ejection fraction of 60% without any other abnormalities. Which of the following is the end-systolic volume in this patient if his cardiac output is 6 L/min?

To determine the end-systolic volume (ESV) of the patient, we first need to calculate the stroke volume (SV) using the provided cardiac output (CO) and heart rate (HR). The cardiac output is given as 6 L/min, and the heart rate is 100 beats/min. Using the formula SV = CO / HR, we calculate the stroke volume as 60 mL/beat (6000 mL/min divided by 100 beats/min).

Given the ejection fraction (EF) of 60%, we can calculate the end-diastolic volume (EDV) using the relationship EF = SV / EDV. Rearranging this formula gives EDV = SV / EF. Substituting the known values, EDV = 60 mL / 0.60 = 100 mL.

The end-systolic volume (ESV) can then be calculated using the formula ESV = EDV - SV. Substituting the values, ESV = 100 mL - 60 mL = 40 mL.
